opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to frame it is that the economics flip once the agent is working in the background rather than in front of you. When you're sitting there in a chat, you're paying with your attention: every second of latency, every wrong turn, you feel it. With a background agent, you've handed off the task and you come back later, so the real question becomes whether the result was worth what it cost. Quality matters far more than speed.

That changes how much you're willing to delegate. If the agent can spend more compute, do more research, check its own work, and come back with something you can actually trust, then you start handing it things you'd never have bothered automating: the long-tail tasks, the "I'd love to know this but it's not worth three hours of my time" questions. The value side opens up a lot of latent demand.

On cost, I don't think the right model is "make it as cheap as possible." It's more that people want a dial. For some tasks you want a fast, cheap answer that's roughly right. For others, like a diligence question or something going into a decision, you're happy to pay a lot more, maybe wait longer, for something meaningfully more accurate and better sourced. When the cost tracks the value of the task, delegation goes up across the board, because you're no longer forcing one price point onto very different kinds of work.

The limiting factor ends up being trust more than cost. You delegate as much as you can verify, or as much as you trust without verifying. So the systems that win will be the ones that are transparent about how they got an answer and where it came from, so you can calibrate. As that trust builds, I think the amount of work people hand off grows much faster than we expect, because most knowledge work today is constrained by human time, not by how much work is actually worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses handing off tasks and latent demand, but does not describe one-time setup creating recurring search work for later meetings.

r002.rationale: It says delegation increases when an agent’s result is worth its cost, and that people may spend more compute when it produces more trustworthy, valuable results.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute tolerance for overspending to the absolute cost still being small.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to a pretty simple economic loop, and the interesting part is that both sides of it are moving at the same time.

On the value side, the thing that matters is how much you trust the output when it comes back. A background agent is only useful if the thing it hands you is something you'd actually accept without redoing it. Right now, for a lot of tasks, people are verifying so heavily that the delegation barely saves time. But as the quality goes up, the verification cost goes down, and that's when the behavior really changes. You stop thinking of it as "I'll try handing this off" and start thinking of it as "why would I ever do this myself?"

On the cost side, the obvious part is that tokens are getting cheaper, and that compounds. But the less obvious part is that the cost of a background agent isn't really the compute. It's the cognitive overhead of specifying the task, waiting, and then reviewing. If I have to write a perfect spec, that's expensive. If I have to babysit it, that's expensive. So the agents that win are the ones that lower that overhead, where you can give a somewhat vague instruction, go do something else, and come back to something that's mostly right.

What I actually expect is that as both of those curves move, delegation becomes the default rather than the exception. Today you delegate the things you don't want to do. Pretty soon you delegate everything that doesn't require your specific judgment, and you spend your time on framing problems and deciding between options rather than executing. And honestly, once the cost gets low enough, you don't delegate one agent per task. You spin up five in parallel on different approaches and pick the best one. That's a very different way of working, and I think most people haven't internalized yet how quickly we're going to get there.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention one-time agent setup or recurring search work for later meetings.

r002.rationale: It describes delegation as an economic tradeoff between value and cost, saying delegation expands as quality rises, verification costs fall, and agent costs become low enough.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute tolerance for potentially excessive agent spending to the spending’s small absolute cost.

astra-6.text:
I think it comes down to the value of the work relative to the cost of getting it done. And cost isn’t just compute. It’s also the time I spend explaining the task, providing context, and checking the result. If an agent takes an hour to do something but I have to spend another hour reviewing it, that changes how useful it is.

With background agents, I don’t have to sit there waiting. I can delegate several things and come back to the results. As they become cheaper and more reliable, I’d expect to delegate work that I wouldn’t otherwise have done at all—exploring another approach, checking an assumption, investigating a question that wasn’t quite worth my time.

So I don’t think it’s a fixed amount of work that gradually moves to agents. The amount of work we choose to do can grow. But that depends on the results being valuable and the effort of supervising them staying low.

r001.rationale: The response discusses delegating tasks to background agents, but does not say that a one-time setup creates recurring search work for later meetings.

r002.rationale: It says delegation depends on the value of the work relative to its cost, including compute, and that more work will be delegated as agents become cheaper if results remain valuable.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute tolerance for potentially excessive agent spending to the absolute cost still being small.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it comes down to how much value an agent creates relative to the cost of running it and checking its work. If I can hand off a task and get back something useful with very little supervision, I’ll delegate a lot more. If I have to spend as much time reviewing the result as I would have spent doing it myself, the economics are much less compelling.

Background agents also change what work we consider worth doing. There are things you never get around to because they’re individually too small or speculative. As the cost comes down, you can have agents explore those possibilities in parallel. So I don’t think it’s just a question of what fraction of my existing work I delegate. It’s also how much additional useful work becomes possible.
